text: Project 3 is finished when a stranger can open your work, understand the problem in a minute, and trust the numbers. This lesson closes it: a one-page result, a review checklist, a final presentation to your instructor as VP of Sales, and a portfolio write-up. All figures are illustrative.

Start with the one-page result for Alder and Vale. Sales: 5.4 million won, 60 percent of quota, 2.0 times coverage, 27 percent win rate, 19 stalled deals worth 2.1 million. Service: 640 opened, 598 closed, backlog up 42 to 187, 71 percent within target. If you can't say each side in a sentence, you're not finished.

Run a checklist before anyone else sees it. Every KPI has a definition and a date range. Every filter is tested on every component. You know the running user and the refresh time. Your cleaning steps are documented. The story fits in three sentences. And you've previewed it on a phone.

Then the final presentation, about five minutes. The answer first. Three findings. One recommendation. Then questions, where you use the pushback pattern: listen, restate, answer with data or a definition, and park what you can't answer. Keep the one-page result as your backup.

Your portfolio write-up has five sections. The problem and audience. The data and approach. Your design decisions. Results, with screenshots of your own dashboard. And limits with next steps. Use a developer org or sample data, never confidential employer data.

Be honest about limits. Each component draws on one report. The quota may be a value you maintain by hand. History needs trend reporting or snapshots. Each limit is evidence for what comes next, whether a stored quota field, snapshots, or CRM Analytics or Tableau.
You now have three portfolio projects. Next chapter, we turn them into interview answers, starting with the questions Salesforce analyst interviews commonly ask.
